verdict.rationale: The New Testament lexical pattern across the four anchor passages is convergent and exclusivist with no opening for parallel saving paths. John 14:6 pairs the emphatic 'I am' (ego eimi) with three nouns introduced by 'the' (articular predicate nominatives, that is, nouns completing a 'X is Y' statement): 'the way' (he hodos), 'the truth' (he aletheia), 'the life' (he zoe), and then closes every route with 'no one comes to the Father except through me' (oudeis erchetai pros ton patera ei me di emou), a universal negation plus a single exceptive clause. Acts 4:12 stacks four negators: 'not' (ouk), 'in no one' (oudeni), 'neither' (oude), and the impersonal 'it is necessary' (dei) around two distinct words for 'other', namely 'other' of the same kind (allos, numerical other) and 'other' of a different kind (heteros, qualitatively other), binding salvation to the one 'name' (onoma). 1 Timothy 2:5 applies the numeral 'one' (heis) twice, 'one God' (heis theos) and 'one mediator' (heis mesites), so that a single go-between is mathematically fixed. 1 John 5:11-12 ties 'eternal life' (zoe aionios) to the Son with a participial antithesis, 'the one having' (ho echon) and 'the one not having' (ho me echon), and the negation 'does not have the life' (ten zoen ouk echei). The denial of pluralism (that other religions are independent saving paths) is therefore strongly grounded. A separate, lexically distinct sub-question (whether saving access requires explicit faith in Christ, the exclusivist reading, or may reach some who never heard, the inclusivist reading) is left open by these words, because both readings still route salvation through the one named Christ and so both deny pluralism.

scripture.force: 'I am the way and the truth and the life' (Ego eimi he hodos kai he aletheia kai he zoe) is followed by 'no one comes to the Father except through me' (oudeis erchetai pros ton patera ei me di emou). The emphatic 'I am' (ego eimi) with three 'the'-marked nouns completing a 'X is Y' statement (articular predicate nominatives) identifies Jesus as the singular path, and the universal negation 'no one' (oudeis) paired with the exceptive 'except' (ei me) plus the 'from-X' or agency form 'through me' (di emou, a genitive of agency, that is, a noun in the 'from-X' grammatical form marking the means) closes every alternative route to the Father. Queried token data confirms 'no one' (oudeis, G3762), 'not' (me, G3361), and 'through' (dia, G1223) are all present in the verse.

'There is salvation in no one else' (Ouk estin en allo oudeni he soteria), with the layered negation 'not' (ouk) plus 'in no one' (oudeni) and the locative 'in another' (en allo), denies saving effect to any other source. The follow-up 'for neither is there another name ... by which it is necessary that we be saved' (oude gar onoma estin heteron ... en ho dei sothenai hemas) adds 'neither' (oude) and the qualitatively other 'another of a different kind' (heteron), then the impersonal 'it is necessary' (dei) and the completed-past passive infinitive (aorist passive infinitive, that is, the 'to be done once' form in passive voice) 'to be saved' (sothenai) bind salvation to the single 'name'. The verse uses BOTH 'other of the same kind' (allos, G0243, numerically another) and 'other of a different kind' (heteros, G2087, another of a different kind), foreclosing other paths on both axes. Queried glosses: 'other' (allos) is other or another, and 'other' (heteros) is the distributive other denoting the second of a pair.

'For there is one God and one mediator between God and humans, the human Christ Jesus' (Heis gar theos, heis kai mesites theou kai anthropon, anthropos Christos Iesous). The numeral 'one' (heis) applied to both 'God' (theos) and 'mediator' (mesites) is mathematically exclusive: a single mediator between God and humans is named, leaving no slot for parallel mediators. 'Mediator' (mesites, G3316) occurs only 6 times in the New Testament (here, Galatians 3:19, Galatians 3:20, Hebrews 8:6, Hebrews 9:15, Hebrews 12:24), always a covenant go-between, with the queried gloss 'arbitrator, mediator' and a Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint, LXX) background in Job 9:33; its sense is low-frequency but stable, not ambiguous.

'God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son' (Zoen aionion edoken hemin ho theos, kai haute he zoe en to huio autou estin). The completed past tense form 'he gave' (edoken, an aorist, that is, a completed past action) locates the gift and the locative 'in his Son' (en to huio) binds eternal life to the Son as its exclusive container. Queried token data confirms 'life' (zoe, G2222), 'eternal' (aionios, G0166), 'son' (huios, G5207), and 'to give' (didomi, G1325) are present.

'The one having the Son has the life; the one not having the Son of God does not have the life' (Ho echon ton huion echei ten zoen, ho me echon ton huion tou theou ten zoen ouk echei). The participial antithesis between 'having' (echon) and 'not having' (me echon), sealed by the negation 'not ... does not have' (me ... ouk echei, the one not having does not have), excludes life from anyone lacking the Son. Queried data confirms 'to have' (echo, G2192), 'not' (me, G3361), and 'not' (ou, G3756) together in the verse.

'In every nation the one fearing him and working righteousness is acceptable to him' (En panti ethnei ho phoboumenos auton kai ergazomenos dikaiosynen dektos auto estin). The phrase 'acceptable' (dektos) applied across every 'nation' (ethnos) is the strongest lexical foothold for an inclusivist reading. It says God accepts the God-fearer who works righteousness in any nation, but the vocabulary does not name an alternative saving path. In the immediate narrative Peter still proceeds to preach the name, so 'acceptable' (dektos) describes whom God receives, not a second mechanism of salvation independent of Christ.

complicating_texts.resolution: 'The one fearing him and working righteousness is acceptable to him' (Ho phoboumenos auton kai ergazomenos dikaiosynen dektos auto estin) uses 'acceptable' (dektos), not 'to save' (sozo) or 'salvation' (soteria). The verse establishes that God shows no partiality across nations and receives the God-fearer, which the inclusivist lens reads as room for those who never heard. But the vocabulary names no second saving path. Cornelius still hears and believes the preached name in the same narrative, so 'acceptable' (dektos) describes divine impartiality in whom God draws, consistent with the one Mediator of 1 Timothy 2:5, not a parallel religion.

Queried key terms are 'nation' or Gentiles (ethnos), 'law' (nomos), 'conscience' (syneidesis), 'to defend' (apologeomai), 'to accuse' (kategoreo). The conscience either accuses or excuses on judgment day. Crucially Romans 2:16 reads 'God judges the secrets of humans ... through Christ Jesus' (krinei ho theos ta krypta ton anthropon ... dia Christou Iesou), so the scene is judicial and still routed 'through Christ' (dia Christou). It supplies grounds for accountability, not an independent saving path, and Romans 3 concludes 'none is righteous' and salvation is 'through faith in Jesus Christ' (dia pisteos Iesou Christou).

'I have other sheep that are not of this fold' (Alla probata echo ha ouk estin ek tes aules tautes) uses 'other' (allos, here in the plural for 'other sheep') but then 'there will be one flock, one shepherd' (genesontai mia poimne, heis poimen), one flock, one shepherd. Queried terms 'one' (heis, G1520), 'shepherd' (poimen, G4166), 'flock' (poimne, G4167) confirm the singular shepherd and flock. The other sheep belong to the same Shepherd, reinforcing single-path gathering rather than a second path.

'The living God, who is the Savior of all humans, especially believers' (Theos zon hos estin soter panton anthropon, malista piston). The genuine lexical seam here is the multiple-sense range of the 'savior' (soter) and 'salvation' (soteria) word group, whose queried gloss includes 'deliverance', 'preservation', 'safety' as well as end-times salvation. The qualifier 'especially' (malista) followed by 'believers' (piston) marks a narrowing, so the universal sense reads as God the preserver of all while saving faith is reserved for believers, tied back to the 'one mediator' (heis mesites) rather than universalizing saving access.

variant_units_examined.note: The SBLGNT apparatus (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) carries a marker on the article and verb form in the surrounding text, but no witness drops the exclusive 'except through me' (ei me di emou) clause. The exclusive force is uniform across the textual tradition.

The apparatus shows an 'neither' (oude) or 'not' (ou) variation marker and a word-order marker around 'under heaven' (hypo ton ouranon), but the negation pattern and the binding of 'salvation' (soteria) to the one 'name' (onoma) persist in all readings.
The apparatus shows variation in pronoun and word order around 'he gave us' (edoken hemin), but the claim binding 'eternal life' (zoe aionios) to the Son is stable across witnesses.

variants.note: The cited verses (John 14, Acts 4, 1 Timothy 2, 1 John 5) are outside the ingested ECM (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) window, which currently covers only 3 John 1:1 to 1:15. The flag not_in_ecm_scope is true for all anchors, so variant assessment rests on SBLGNT and Nestle1904 apparatus markers, which is recorded as 'ecm-shadow' rather than 'ecm-published'.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads 'I am the way' (ego eimi he hodos), 'in no one else' (ouk en allo oudeni), and 'one mediator' (heis mesites) at face value and holds that saving access comes only through explicit faith in the named Christ. The negations and numeric singularity exclude alternative saving paths, and Acts 4:12 ties 'salvation' (soteria) to the 'name' (onoma, the named Christ), which on this reading requires the name to be known and trusted.

Holds that Christ is the only Savior and the only ground of salvation, so it equally denies pluralism, but reads Acts 10:35 ('acceptable' (dektos) in every nation) and Romans 2:14-16 (conscience that may excuse) as leaving lexical room for Christ's saving work to reach some who never heard the name explicitly. On this reading the one Mediator of 1 Timothy 2:5 still mediates, but the application is not strictly limited to those with explicit knowledge.

Holds that multiple religions are independent saving paths. The Greek pattern of 'no one ... except' (oudeis ... ei me), 'not ... in no one else' (ouk ... en allo oudeni), 'neither ... another' (oude ... heteron), 'one mediator' (heis mesites), and 'the one not having ... does not have' (me echon ... ouk echei) systematically forecloses this reading. No lexical hook in any anchor verse supports a multi-path salvation theology, so this lens is the one the texts directly negate.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict on pluralism and the exclusivist-versus-inclusivist sub-question are lexically distinct. The anchors layer four independent negation strategies ('no one ... except' (oudeis ei me); 'not in no one' (ouk en oudeni) with both 'other of the same kind' (allos) and 'other of a different kind' (heteros); the numeric 'one' (heis); and 'the one not having ... does not have' (me echon ... ouk echei)) that together deny pluralism redundantly. They do NOT settle whether the saving work reaches only those who explicitly believe or also some who never heard, because Acts 10:35 'acceptable' (dektos) and Romans 2:14-16 'conscience' (syneidesis) use vocabulary that names neither an alternative path (which would help pluralism) nor an explicit-faith requirement (which would settle exclusivism). Both exclusivism and inclusivism deny pluralism; their internal disagreement is a separate question the words underdetermine.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Salvation is found exclusively through Christ, and no other religion or path provides independent saving access to God.
stem_audit.notes: This is a DENIAL stem (pluralism is the error denied). The proposition is phrased in terms the New Testament itself uses (sole mediator, no other name, no other way, no one comes except through me), so it is not preloaded with a tradition-specific taxonomy; a tradition-neutral rephrasing is supplied for transparency. The verdict is derived on the original stem. The stem targets pluralism specifically and does not prejudge the distinct exclusivist-versus-inclusivist sub-question, which is left open in the lens analysis.

lay_summary: The four anchor passages converge on one lexical pattern. In John 14:6 Jesus says 'I am the way, the truth, the life' (ego eimi he hodos, he aletheia, he zoe), an emphatic 'I am' with three 'the'-marked nouns, and then 'no one' (oudeis) comes to the Father except 'through' (dia) him. The negation is universal and the exception is single. In Acts 4:12 Peter stacks negators. There is no salvation 'in no one else' (en allo oudeni), and no other 'name' (onoma) under heaven by which it is necessary to be saved. The Greek pointedly uses both 'another of the same kind' (allos) and 'another of a different kind' (heteros), so it closes off other names on both axes. In 1 Timothy 2:5 the numeral 'one' (heis) appears twice, one God and one 'mediator' (mesites), and 'mediator' is a precise go-between word that occurs only six times, leaving no room for parallel mediators. In 1 John 5:11-12 eternal life is bound to the Son, and whoever does not have the Son does not have the life. Four passages, four independent ways of saying no, one consistent result. This is why the denial of pluralism, the claim that other religions are separate saving paths, is strongly grounded. The text negates that directly. There is, however, a second and different question the same words do not settle, and this is where careful readers diverge. Acts 10:35 says the God-fearer who works righteousness is 'acceptable' (dektos) in every nation, and Romans 2 describes a conscience that can excuse, yet both verses route everything back through Christ (Romans 2:16 says God judges through Christ Jesus) and neither names a rival path. So one reader concludes saving access requires explicitly hearing and trusting the name, while another concludes the one Savior may still reach some who never heard. Notice that both of those readers still deny pluralism, because both keep Christ as the only Savior. The vocabulary clearly rules out many independent paths, but it does not by itself rule on the reach of the single path, partly because the 'savior' (soter) word group can mean preserver as well as end-times savior, as in 1 Timothy 4:10. That distinction explains the divergence without weakening the core verdict.

license_audit.non_redistributable_reason: MACULA-Greek is CC-BY-NC-4.0 and SBLGNT-text is under SBLGNT-EULA, and both restrict bulk redistribution. The syntactic anchoring of the negation constructions and the Greek base text rely on these sources, so the composite evidence cannot be published in bulk without rebuilding the morphology and syntax layer from purely public-domain and CC-BY tier sources.
